Article Title: New York City's Knicks emailed employees free NBA championship rings, it was not what it seemed; MSG says: Using the rings as a lure to gain employees' attention was...
Article Text:
The Knicks championship ring email was built to look official

MSG says a real phishing attack led to the test

Prize-themed phishing tests draw clicks, but security agencies warn against punishing staff

Madison Square Garden Sports, the parent company of the New York Knicks, has admitted that an email offering staff free NBA championship rings was a phishing test. Employees who clicked to reserve a ring were sent to a mandatory cybersecurity class instead.The company has now called it an "unfortunate mistake." It says it will hand out more than 275 championship rings and pieces of jewellery, worth over $3.7 million, to players, coaches, employees and others in the organisation. The timing made the episode sting. The Knicks won the 2026 NBA title in June, their first since 1973, and the franchise is still in the middle of celebrating it.The email went out to a long list of MSG employees in late September, weeks before the team's ring-and-banner ceremony. According to The Athletic, which obtained a copy, it opened with a graphic of two ring styles and the line "Congratulations, your Employee Championship Ring is here."Each employee was addressed by name and told the ring was complimentary, personalised and made by the same jeweller as the players' rings. There were two designs to pick from: Championship Gold and Garden Classic.It was an easy offer to believe. Most NBA team employees receive a ring after a title, even if it is a simpler version of what the players wear.Team sources told The Athletic that those who clicked were put through a cybersecurity class tied to owner James Dolan's growing concerns about hacking.MSG's first response to The Athletic was short: "We are not disclosing anything about the rings." A day later, the company changed course. A spokesperson said the email was a phishing simulation sent to the corporate team to strengthen its security against hackers."MSG was recently hacked and extorted using an employee login and password obtained through a similar phishing attack," the statement said. It added that using the rings as a lure "was an unfortunate mistake."Phishing drills are routine at large companies, so the criticism is mostly about the bait. Guidance from the US National Institute of Standards and Technology says such exercises should not be punitive. GoDaddy faced a similar backlash in 2020, when a fake holiday bonus email to staff turned out to be a security test.From a pure security standpoint, the ring was an effective lure. Attackers often dress up phishing emails as rewards because people act on them quickly and without much thought. In a recent report, Kaspersky found that a FIFA-themed phishing simulation offering prizes for wearing a national team jersey got a 66% click rate.The trouble lies in what happens after the click. The UK's National Cyber Security Centre says punishing employees for falling for a test email can start to look like entrapment. It also advises companies to check with HR before sending anything that could upset staff, which a fake championship ring offer was always likely to do.Security tech has been a sore point at MSG for a while. The Garden has used facial recognition at its entrances since at least 2018, and in 2023 it was reported to have used the system to turn away lawyers from firms involved in litigation against the company. A database leaked earlier this year also showed MSG assigning risk scores to celebrities and their guests.MSG has not said how many employees clicked the September email, or whether it plans to change how it runs these tests.
Article Summary: The email went out to a long list of MSG employees in late September, weeks before the team's ring-and-banner ceremony. It opened with a graphic of two ring styles and the line "Congratulations, your Employee Championship Ring is here" The company has now called it an "unfortunate mistake" and says it will hand out more than 275 rings and pieces of jewellery.

Article Title: In 2025, a developer proposed a $3.6 billion data center across 133 acres in Ohio and filed plans before a local ban; on October 20, the state Supreme Court ruled the village could keep the project on
Article Text:
Developer raced to file plans before restrictions

The timeline

Court sides with village

Massive AI-era data centre proposal

Local opposition and wider trend

A proposed $3.6 billion data centre campus in Ohio will remain on hold after the Supreme Court of Ohio ruled that local officials in the village of Lordstown do not have to continue reviewing the project while a moratorium on new data centres remains in effect. The decision stems from a dispute involving Bristolville 25 Developer LLC, which is seeking to build four three-storey data centre buildings and related infrastructure on industrial land in Lordstown, about 45 miles southeast of Cleveland. According to court records and industry reports, the development has been valued at approximately $3.6 billion and would span 133 acres across the Trumbull-Mahoning county lineThe developer began Lordstown's site-plan review process in October 2025, submitting initial plans just days before village officials moved to restrict new data centre developments. The following day, the village's planning and zoning administrator informed the company that a ban on data centres was being considered by the village council.In November 2025, Lordstown approved a ban on new data centres. The village later repealed the outright ban and replaced it with a six-month moratorium in January 2026 before extending the moratorium through the remainder of 2026.Bristolville argued that because its plans were submitted when data centres were still permitted under local zoning rules, the project should continue to be reviewed under the earlier regulations.The company sought a writ of mandamus compelling the village to move forward with the approval process.Bristolville bought the land in February 2025 and delivered its draft site plan on October 20, 2025. The next day, the village’s planning and zoning administrator told the company that a data center ban was pending before council and that review could not begin until council decided. About 100 residents, mostly opposed to new data centers, attended a council meeting in November 2025, and council voted 6-0 to ban new data centers.In January 2026, the village replaced the ban with a six-month moratorium, and council later extended it through the rest of 2026. The village engineer did an initial review after the ban passed and found missing information, including stormwater management and utility plans. Once the ban became a moratorium, the village suspended further review, and the company asked the Supreme Court to compel it to continue.In a unanimous decision issued on October 20, the state's highest court rejected the developer's claim. The court found that Bristolville had only initiated the first stage of Lordstown's four-step review process and had not completed the requirements necessary to obtain the right to apply for a zoning permit.The court concluded that because the developer had not advanced far enough through the approval process before the moratorium took effect, village officials were under no legal obligation to continue reviewing the project.Planning documents described the proposed facility as a 1.65 million-square-foot campus featuring four three-storey data centre buildings. During public discussions, project representatives said the facility would use closed-loop cooling systems and could employ around 120 people across three shifts once completed.The developer's engineering team also indicated that cooling water would initially be trucked to the site, while discussions had been held with utility provider FirstEnergy regarding the project's electricity requirements"Under the moratorium, the village is under no legal duty to proceed with a site-plan review," the court stated in its opinion.The proposal attracted significant local attention. According to reports, around 100 residents attended a village council meeting in November 2025, with most expressing opposition to additional data centre development. Village leaders said the moratorium was intended to give officials time to study potential regulations and assess the impact of such projects on the community.The ruling also adds to a series of setbacks for projects linked to Western Hospitality Partners, the New York-based company affiliated with Bristolville 25 Developer. Several proposed data centre campuses in other US states have reportedly faced opposition, zoning hurdles or infrastructure-related challenges.For now, the Ohio Supreme Court's ruling means the Lordstown project will remain frozen while the village's moratorium remains in place
Article Summary: Bristolville 25 Developer LLC is seeking to build four three-storey data centre buildings and related infrastructure on industrial land in Lordstown, Ohio. The development has been valued at approximately $3.6 billion and would span 133 acres across the Trumbull-Mahoning county line. The developer began Lordstown's site-plan review process in October 2025, submitting initial plans just days before village officials moved to restrict new data centre developments. In November 2025, Lordstown approved a ban on new data centres. The village later repealed the outright ban and replaced it with a six-month moratorium in January

Article Title: ‘The tensile fibers act like tethers’, says Nike’s Bret Schoolmeester on the science inside Apex’s Air Zoom units
Article Text:
Nike’s Apex marathon racer stacks four Air Zoom units under the forefoot

What a new weld means for the Air Zoom unit

Apex spends its whole 40mm allowance on the forefoot

Nike has spent decades learning what Air can do, and its new racers lean on it harder than ever. Apex, the marathon racer due in January 2027, packs four Air Zoom units into two stacked pairs under the forefoot, the most Air Nike has placed there, and Alphafly 4 runs a pair of the same new unit. It is a confident bet, given that Air Zoom took much of the blame when the Pegasus Premium and Vomero Premium turned out heavier than runners expected.Bret Schoolmeester, Nike’s Vice President of Running Footwear, explains the bet in four words. “Air is highly tunable,” he says. Nike can engineer a unit’s size, shape, pressure and placement around the ride it wants, and weight turned out to be one more thing it could tune.An Air Zoom unit is a sealed polymer bag of pressurised gas that compresses as the forefoot loads it and pushes back as the runner pushes off. Tensile fibres run between its top and bottom surfaces like tethers, letting Nike pressurise it hard while keeping it flat. Schoolmeester calls it “one of the highest-energy-return cushioning technologies we have tested”. Foam slowly packs out, while a sealed unit is designed to hold its behaviour for as long as it is worn.The weight fix came from the way the shell is sealed. Nike used to form the unit with heat and has moved to radio-frequency welding, which uses a high-frequency electromagnetic field to heat certain polymers from within, right at the joint. A much thinner film can be sealed that way without losing the tensile-fibre structure, and each unit came out 30 percent lighter.Getting there took what Schoolmeester has described as urgency and sleepless nights. “Confidence grew as the process repeatedly delivered consistent results, first in development and then through athlete testing,” he says, though he did not go into how every sealed unit is checked on the line.A lighter unit solved only half the problem. Apex also needed room. World Athletics caps the sole of a road racer at 40mm, insole included, and an 8mm drop maxed out at the heel leaves just 32mm under the forefoot. Apex is zero-drop at 40mm in both places, handing the whole allowance to the forefoot, where the stacked Air sits. “Zero-drop is more about the maximum propulsion in the forefoot,” Schoolmeester says.Everything else is tuned around that stack. Simulations showed two units on top of each other gave the best balance of energy return and stability. ZoomX LT foam sits beneath them, and above them a comparatively flat carbon-fibre Flyplate pushes load down so the units compress properly. The rocker and the stability come from the geometry of the whole platform, helped by a wider outsole. “Stability doesn’t necessarily come from adding more material, it comes from how you use the material you have,” he says.Nike’s numbers are up to 40 percent more energy return than Alphafly 3 at more than 10 percent less weight. The zero-drop is worth watching, since a lower drop generally asks more of the calves and Achilles, though wear testers logged more than 160km in Apex. Durability has not moved either, with Nike’s expectation for Alphafly 4 level with Alphafly 3.Nike will not say how much of that 40 percent belongs to Air, because it measures the whole system, and Swooshfly shows why. The more accessible racer has no Air Zoom at all and relies on SkyX, a foam of TPU beads steamed to different densities around the heel, plate and forefoot, which Nike compares to tuned Air. “Air Zoom and foam each offer different ways to tune a ride,” Schoolmeester says.Not long ago, Air’s weight was its limit, and a change in the factory moved it. Schoolmeester does not think Nike has reached the next one. “We do not think we have found the limits of Air yet,” he says.
Article Summary: Nike’s Apex marathon racer stacks four Air Zoom units under the forefoot. It is the most Air Nike has placed there, and Alphafly 4 runs a pair of the same new unit. Air Zoom took much of the blame when the Pegasus Premium and Vomero Premium turned out heavier than runners expected. The weight fix came from the way the shell is sealed.

Article Title: Xbox's first COO Helen Chiang leaves Microsoft after 21 years, just months after promotion; CEO Asha Sharma in memo to employees: I am ...
Article Text:
“Helen Chiang is leaving Microsoft today. I’m grateful for her years of service and wish her well,”

“We’ll share more on COO leadership as plans are finalised,”

“We don’t discuss individual personnel matters,”

“We’re grateful for Helen’s years of service and wish her well.”

Why Xbox created its first COO position

“end-to-end P&L responsibility across content, hardware, platform, and services.”

Microsoft has lost Xbox’s first chief operating officer. Helen Chiang left the company after 21 years, about three months after she was promoted to the newly created position in July. Xbox CEO Asha Sharma announced the departure in an internal memo, but Microsoft did not explain why Chiang was leaving.Sharma told employees in a memo reviewed by The Verge. She did not name a replacement but indicated that Xbox would retain COO leadership.she added.Microsoft also declined to explain the circumstances surrounding her exit.Xbox communications vice president Kari Perez told The Verge.As COO, Chiang was responsible for bringing Xbox’s content, hardware, platform and services businesses under one operating structure. Other Xbox leaders will divide her duties until the company finalises its plans for the position.Chiang was promoted as part of a wider reorganisation that Xbox described as a business reset. At the time, Sharma said the new position would carryP&L refers to profit-and-loss responsibility, meaning Chiang was expected to oversee how those parts of Xbox earned money, controlled costs and made investment decisions.Sharma said Chiang would “bring our businesses together under one operating model, making sure we make clear investment decisions, learn from our successes and failures, and hold ourselves accountable for results.”Her departure does not appear to end the COO position. For now, other Xbox leaders will handle her immediate responsibilities while the company finalises its plans.Chiang joined Microsoft in 2005 as a product manager for its Streets & Trips mapping software and moved to Xbox in 2007. She joined the Minecraft team in 2014, later became its studio head, and served as corporate vice president of the franchise. GamesRadar reported that her Xbox career included work on Xbox Live and leadership of Mojang and Minecraft.
Article Summary: Helen Chiang was promoted to the newly created position in July. She was responsible for bringing Xbox’s content, hardware, platform and services businesses under one operating structure. Other Xbox leaders will divide her duties until the company finalises its plans for the position.

Article Title: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang says US regulation pushed China’s domestic capabilities but America's technology is ....
Article Text:
Jensen Huang.

US export curbs on China

‘American technology well prepared’

‘Companies can always use more RAM’

Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang has said that export curbs and trade restrictions imposed by Washington have served as a ‘catalyst’ for China’s rapid progress in semiconductor development. Speaking to CNBC on the sidelines of Nvidia's GTC Berlin conference, Huang stated that American regulatory measures effectively pushed China to speed up its own domestic chip manufacturing and strive for technological self-reliance. The top executive also dismissed concerns over a memory chip glut, saying that a supply surplus is unlikely to materialise by 2029.Current US trade rules prohibit the export of advanced processors to China, including Nvidia's high-end artificial intelligence (AI) GPUs. Despite these barriers, reports have claimed, several Chinese entities have managed to access that computing power through third-party data centers based in Southeast Asia. Industry experts consider this access crucial to the growing capabilities of Chinese-developed AI models.“We’ve definitely accelerated China’s initiatives, its nationalization of semiconductor manufacturing capabilities, and all of the industrial support that has been put into that sector, and so there’s no question we’ve accelerated that,” Huang said.Even with intensified competition and China’s accelerated domestic initiatives, the Nvidia chief expressed strong confidence in the standing of US technology companies. Huang stated that American tech firms remain “mighty” and are well-prepared to take on competitive pressure “from anybody.”Rejecting concerns that memory chips will be supply surplus, Huang implied that the ongoing hardware supercycle is not nearing any abrupt end."One of the things that's really great about memory is that you can always use more of it," Huang said,underscoring that High Bandwidth Memory (HBM), which is a specialised form of RAM critical for Al acceleration, will continue to see widespread use for years to come.“We're the first company in the world to put LPDDR memory - what goes into your cell phones - into the world's data centers, and it's enabled us to deliver performance that's twice as energy efficient as anything in the world today, and so we're going to continue to use abundant amounts of them as well,” he said.
Article Summary: Jensen Huang says export curbs and trade restrictions imposed by Washington have served as a ‘catalyst’ for China’s rapid progress in semiconductor development. Huang also dismissed concerns over a memory chip glut, saying that a supply surplus is unlikely to materialise by 2029.

Article Title: Mark Zuckerberg and Priscilla Chan said that they shifting their donations, just weeks after Meta CEO gifted state of California ...
Article Text:
$50 million gift backs AI and STEM expansion

The billionaire tax backdrop

Philanthropic strategy undergoes major shift

AI at the centre of both Meta and CZI

Layoffs accompany new focus

Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg and his wife Priscilla Chan are doubling down on artificial intelligence, science and STEM education through both their philanthropic and corporate investments, according to a Fortune report. The couple ledged $50 million to Sacramento State University to pay for state-of-the-art STEM labs and an AI center, Fortune reports. California Governor Gavin Newsom announced the gift on January 28 and tied it to a major redevelopment of three vacant state office buildings on Sacramento’s Capitol Mall into a downtown campus. The money from Zuckerberg and Meta will cover abatement, demolition and initial construction, and will make room for new student housing alongside academic space, including STEM facilities and the AI center. Zuckerberg said the investments will strengthen communities and support the next generation of leaders and innovators. Newsom said the gift will help the school build its pipeline of talent for tech jobs, and that students need to be able to afford to live where they study.California Governor Gavin Newsom announced the donation on January 28 as part of a broader plan to transform three vacant state office buildings on Sacramento's Capitol Mall into a downtown university campus.The contribution from Meta and Zuckerberg will help fund demolition, site preparation and the initial construction phase of the project.The new campus is expected to include advanced STEM laboratories, an AI centre and student housing, with state officials framing the project as an investment in California's future workforce. Newsom said the donation would help Sacramento State strengthen its pipeline of talent for technology jobs and support students by expanding affordable housing options near campus. In a statement cited by the report, Zuckerberg said the investments would help "strengthen our communities and support the next generation of leaders and innovators. "The gift arrives as California considers a one-time 5 percent tax on billionaires’ wealth. Fortune notes that several prominent billionaires, including Google co-founders Larry Page and Sergey Brin, Oracle co-founder Larry Ellison, PayPal co-founder Peter Thiel and Craft Ventures’ David Sacks, have already moved their permanent residences out of state to avoid it. Zuckerberg has made no public statement on the tax and is instead putting more money into California. He owns a compound of 11 properties in Palo Alto’s Crescent Park neighbourhood, valued at more than $110 million, and Meta has a 57-acre headquarters campus in the area plus more than 400,000 square feet of office space in nearby Menlo Park.The Sacramento donation reflects a broader change in direction at the Chan Zuckerberg Initiative (CZI), the philanthropic organisation launched by Zuckerberg and Chan in 2015. The couple recently announced that the majority of CZI's resources would be directed toward biomedical AI research, marking a shift from earlier priorities such as education and social justice initiatives.The organisation has increasingly focused on using artificial intelligence to accelerate scientific discovery and medical research. Central to that strategy is the Biohub network, a group of biomedical research institutes that aims to advance disease prevention and treatment through cutting-edge technologies.Speaking at a Biohub event in Redwood City last year, Zuckerberg described the Biohub model as one of the most impactful efforts undertaken by the organisation and said it would become the primary focus of its philanthropic work going forward.The latest donation also highlights how Zuckerberg's philanthropic goals are increasingly aligned with Meta's broader AI ambitions. Meta has committed significant resources toward developing advanced AI systems and building infrastructure to support future AI-driven products and services. Similarly, CZI is concentrating on AI-powered biomedical research, supporting work involving large-scale models for applications such as virtual cells, immune system research and disease prediction.The planned AI centre at Sacramento State fits into that vision by helping train future researchers, engineers and technology professionals while expanding access to advanced computing and STEM education.The renewed emphasis on AI and biomedical research has also led to organisational changes. Earlier this year, CZI laid off around 70 employees, primarily at its Redwood City headquarters, as it streamlined operations around its updated mission.Despite those cuts, Zuckerberg and Chan have signalled that they see AI as a transformative force for the coming decade. In a recent blog post, the couple said they were optimistic about the opportunities ahead and believed advances in AI and science could help achieve some of humanity's long-term goals.
Article Summary: The couple ledged $50 million to Sacramento State University to pay for state- of-the-art STEM labs and an AI center. California Governor Gavin Newsom announced the gift on January 28 and tied it to a major redevelopment of three vacant state office buildings on Sacramento’s Capitol Mall. Zuckerberg said the investments will strengthen communities and support the next generation of leaders and innovators.

Article Title: 97% of serious gamers say gaming helps them connect with like-minded people: Infinix-CMR study
Article Text:
Key findings of the Infinix-CMR study

One of the major findings of the survey is that socialising has emerged as one of the leading motivations for mobile gaming. Nearly half of both gaming audiences cite socialising with friends and others as a reason to play, including 45% of Serious Gamers and 51% of Hyper-Casual/Casual Gamers.

For 97% of Serious Gamers, gaming helps them connect with like-minded people and communities. The sentiment is equally strong among Hyper-Casual/Casual Gamers, with 85% agreeing.

Gaming decisions are heavily shaped by trusted circles. Among Serious Gamers, 88% identify friends, family and gaming communities as major influences on their choice of games. This extends to device consideration as well, with word of mouth (67%) and recommendations from friends and family (66%) emerging as important influences.

Some of the most meaningful gaming moments happen when friends come together after a long day. The study found that 51% of Serious Gamers and 49% of Hyper-Casual/Casual Gamers stay up late to try game updates or play with friends. That connection also creates a sense of missing out. Around 40% of Serious Gamers report feeling left out when they miss gaming conversations, while 54% of casual gamers experience some level of disconnection. Gaming, for many, has become an ongoing social conversation they want to remain part of.

For Gen Z, how they play is increasingly a reflection of who they are. A 92% of Serious Gamers believe they can express their personality better through gaming. Further, 87% of Serious Gamers and 79% of Hyper-Casual/Casual Gamers say their gaming setup represents their identity. This extends into virtual worlds, with 82% of Serious Gamers saying their in-game avatars, skins and outfits reflect their personal style.

While gamers are investing more time and identity into their gaming experiences, device limitations continue to interrupt play. Battery drain affects 62% of Serious Gamers, while 60% of Hyper-Casual/Casual Gamers report overheating as a concern.

As mentioned above, the survey comes ahead of the Infinix GT 50 Pro launch on October 27. The smartphone is teased to come with its "Game Together" ecosystem, bringing together a gaming smartphone, GT NX Controller, GT NX Station, MagCharge Cooler 2.0 and cloud gaming capabilities.

Gaming is becoming more than just a way to pass time for Gen Z, with most young gamers in India saying it helps them connect with like-minded people. According to a new study by Infinix India and CyberMedia Research (CMR), 97% of serious gamers and 85% of casual gamers said gaming helps them build connections and find communities. The study surveyed 2,057 smartphone users aged 16 to 25 across 16 Indian cities. Released ahead of the Infinix GT 50 Pro launch on October 27, the findings highlight how friendships, shared gaming sessions and online communities are shaping young Indians’ gaming habits.The study examined two distinct gaming audiences: Serious Gamers, who spend more than 12 hours gaming weekly, typically in sessions exceeding 120 minutes, and Hyper-Casual/Casual Gamers, who play up to 11 hours a week, generally in sessions of up to an hour.The findings reveal a generation for whom gaming extends well beyond entertainment. Gaming is no longer a boys’ club. Nearly one in three are women, with female participation reaching 36% among hyper-casual gamers, which reflects how gaming has become a mainstream social activity across gender lines.Miraj Gupta, CMO, Infinix India, said, "For years, conversations around gaming smartphones have largely been about performance, frame rates and benchmarks.But gaming today is also about people. It is friends coming together for a quick gaming session after work, couples finding a new way to spend an evening, or siblings waiting to play their favourite game together. The Infinix–CMR study reinforces what we have been observing: Gen Z doesn't just play games, it plays together. With the GT 50 Pro, we're taking that understanding beyond the smartphone and building an ecosystem that makes gaming more connected, flexible and social. Because the future of mobile gaming isn't just about how well you play, but also about who you play with."Prabhu Ram, Vice President - Industry Research Group, CyberMedia Research (CMR), said, "Gaming is increasingly becoming a way for India’s Gen Z to connect, build communities and express its identity. Its influence extends well beyond gameplay, shaping how young consumers discover games, evaluate devices and personalise their experiences. Yet battery drain and overheating remain persistent constraints. For device makers, the opportunity lies in delivering a more complete gaming experience, where sustained performance complements the social and personal dimensions of play. "
Article Summary: 97% of serious gamers and 85% of casual gamers said gaming helps them build connections and find communities. The study surveyed 2,057 smartphone users aged 16 to 25 across 16 Indian cities. Released ahead of the Infinix GT 50 Pro launch on October 27.

Article Title: Goldman Sachs predicted that AI could displace one in 11 workers, investment banker now gives a timeline on AI layoffs
Article Text:
Goldman Sachs projects up to 9% worker displacement

Recession could be the trigger for AI layoffs

Goldman has issued similar warning before

Historical patterns suggest technology-driven job losses rise during downturns

Why Goldman raised its AI displacement estimate

Why AI layoff fears have eased for now

Artificial intelligence has been at the centre of workforce disruption debates for the past two years, but according to a new analysis from Joseph Briggs, an economist at Goldman Sachs, the biggest impact on jobs may not arrive immediately. Instead, large-scale AI-driven layoffs could accelerate during an economic downturn, even as the current labour market remains relatively resilient. Briggs’s estimate rests on Goldman’s forecast that AI will eventually raise productivity by 15 percent in the US and other developed economies. On that assumption, up to 9 percent of workers could be displaced during the AI transition, or roughly one in 11. Slower hiring could weigh on employment by a further 3 percent.In a research note highlighted by Fortune, Briggs said concerns about immediate AI-related job losses have eased in recent months after reaching a peak earlier this year. However, the economist estimates that if AI ultimately boosts productivity by 15% across the United States and other developed economies, as Goldman Sachs forecasts, up to 9% of workers could be displaced during the transition. Slower hiring linked to AI adoption could weigh on employment by an additional 3%.The estimate means roughly one out of every 11 workers could face displacement as companies increasingly automate tasks and workflows.The report's central argument is that AI's impact on employment is likely to follow a familiar historical pattern. After examining decades of data on technological change and labour markets, Briggs concluded that automation tends to accelerate during economic slowdowns rather than periods of strong growth. "Automation-related labour disruption is limited when the overall economy is healthy but accelerates during cyclical slowdowns," he wrote, according to the Fortune report.The economist warned that AI-related labour disruptions could amplify economic downturns, as companies often use weaker business conditions as an opportunity to reduce labour costs and invest in productivity-enhancing technologies.The latest analysis echoes warnings issued by Goldman Sachs economists David Mericle and Pierfrancesco Mei in October 2025. At the time, they argued that "jobless growth" could become a recurring feature of the economy, where GDP continues to grow but employment expands more slowly. The pair also suggested that the full impact of AI on employment might not become apparent until a recession occurs, allowing companies to restructure workforces more aggressively while implementing automation. According to Briggs, the timing and extent of AI-driven job disruption will likely track broader economic cycles rather than occurring in a sudden wave.The Goldman Sachs analysis points to previous recessions, including the downturns of the early 1980s, 2001, 2008 and 2020, as examples of periods when routine jobs experienced significant declines due to automation. Briggs found that occupations heavily affected by technological change often suffered deeper employment losses when the broader labour market weakened. Across 25 occupations disrupted by past technological shifts, employment fell an additional 4% over five years for every percentage-point increase in the national unemployment rate.The report argues that companies are often more willing to replace labour with technology when economic conditions deteriorate and pressure to cut costs increases.The 9% displacement estimate marks an increase from calculations published by Briggs and economist Sarah Dong in August 2025. At the time, they estimated AI could displace between 6% and 7% of the US workforce under widespread adoption scenarios.In June, speaking on Goldman Sachs' Exchanges podcast, Briggs said the figure could reach around 9%, equal to roughly 15 million workers over a decade. While earlier comments described workers being reallocated to new positions, the latest research note refers to them as displaced workers.Despite the higher projection, Briggs continues to argue that the displacement would be temporary and would not necessarily translate into a dramatic spike in unemployment because some workers would find new jobs relatively quickly while others could leave the workforce entirely.According to the report, one reason widespread AI-related layoffs have not yet materialised is that adoption remains at an early stage. Briggs noted that only 23% of US establishments have incorporated AI into regular workflows, meaning most productivity gains expected from the technology still lie ahead. The economist also pointed to a resilient labour market in 2026. He argued that companies currently have less incentive to aggressively cut jobs because economic conditions have remained relatively stable. Recent indicators cited in the report suggest only modest labour-market effects so far.AI-related layoffs tracked by Challenger have declined from their spring peak, while media coverage of AI-driven job losses has also fallen significantly. Although employment growth in industries most exposed to AI has softened, the impact remains far below earlier fears. Still, Briggs cautioned that a future economic slowdown could change the picture substantially, creating the conditions for companies to accelerate automation efforts and triggering the most significant phase of AI-related workforce disruption.
Article Summary: Goldman Sachs estimates up to 9% of US workforce could be displaced by AI. Slower hiring linked to AI adoption could weigh on employment by an additional 3%. The estimate means roughly one out of every 11 workers could face displacement as companies increasingly automate tasks and workflows.

Article Title: Iran's IRGC threatens to cut undersea internet cables in Persian Gulf: What this may mean for internet users across the globe
Article Text:
Who will be impacted if Iran cuts underwater internet cables

Why cutting cables doesn’t mean cutting internet access globally

Iran’s Revolutionary Guards (IRGC) has once again threatened to target undersea internet cables in the Strait of Hormuz. While the waterway carries only a small share of the world’s internet traffic, damaging its cables will have its impact globally. Notably, the regional impact is likely to be far more severe for countries neighbouring Iran, leaving global internet connectivity largely intact. Yadollah Javani, the Revolutionary Guards’ political deputy, warned this week that vital internet cables in the Strait of Hormuz could be targeted if Iranian infrastructure came under attack.Citing the International Cable Protection Committee (ICPC), a report by Iran International says that five active submarine cable segments pass through the Strait of Hormuz, and together they carry less than 1% of the world’s international bandwidth. It is to be noted that the main data routes linking Europe and East Asia run through the Red Sea. This means that damage to these cables will not have a devastating impact over the internet.TeleGeography says the cables crossing the Strait of Hormuz have been routed through Omani waters because of longstanding political issues and difficult relations with Iran. These cables mainly serve countries in the Persian Gulf, so an attack would be a more immediate threat to regional connectivity than to the wider global internet.Damage to the cables could disrupt international connectivity in Bahrain, Qatar, Kuwait and the United Arab Emirates, though all four have other connections over land. Saudi Arabia depends less on Persian Gulf cable routes, because most of its international bandwidth runs through systems that land on its Red Sea coast.The global internet doesn’t depend on a single network or a single point of failure. Telecom operators use several undersea and land routes to carry data, so if Iran cuts the internet, they can redirect some traffic via other lines. Rerouting may slow speeds, increase delays or disrupt certain services but it doesn’t necessarily cut users off completely.This means the pages may take longer to load, videos may buffer and there may be noticeable delays when refreshing their social media timelines.
Article Summary: Iran's Revolutionary Guards have threatened to target undersea internet cables in the Strait of Hormuz. The waterway carries only a small share of the world’s internet traffic, but damaging its cables will have its impact globally. Article Title: Google Brain cofounder and AI pioneer Andrew Ng tells ‘one of the most disgusting things’ he has seen that AI is being used for
Article Text:
‘Balancing AI’s value with dangerous harms’

Artificial intelligence (AI) pioneer and Google Brain co-founder Andrew Ng has spoken out against malicious applications of the technology, noting the generation of non-consensual deepfake intimate photos as one of the most troubling misuses of modern software he has encountered. Addressing the darker side of technological development in an interview on The Economist's "Inside Tech" podcast recently, the Al pioneer dismissed the notion that this technology presents an existential threat to society.Firstly, Ng delivered a strong critique of synthetic explicit content, calling on lawmakers to establish strict regulations and severe measures to eliminate the abuse entirely.“AI applications have problems. For example, one of the most disgusting things I've ever seen is AI being used to generate non-consensual, deepfake intimate imagery,” Ng said, adding, “That's all for the past laws put in place for harsh penalties to just get rid of that.”While acknowledging the severe harms enabled by certain AI deployments, Ng maintained that the broader technology remains enormously valuable. The primary challenge, he indicated, is addressing harmful cases while preserving the societal benefits created by AI. Despite the prevalence of bad actors and misuse, Ng emphasised that he remains optimistic about the future of AI safety governance.“AI is tremendously valuable, but has some problematic use cases.The thing that gives me optimism is that many nations have managed to collaborate on safety issues, even when they disagreed on other things,” he said.To illustrate how the global community can manage safety risks, Ng pointed to commercial aviation as a proven precedent for cross-border collaboration.“For example, airlines around the world actually do not compete on safety and will share safety information because having aviation be safer is a good thing. Even if airlines are competing like crazy for business, I think there's actually room for collaboration,” Ng added.The founder of DeepLearning Al that provides technical training on Generative Al, Machine Learning, Deep Learning and other topics, also alleged some industry leaders of manufacturing existential safety arguments to lobby for regulations that crush open-source competition.
Article Summary: Google Brain co-founder Andrew Ng has spoken out against malicious applications of the technology. Ng noted the generation of non-consensual deepfake intimate photos as one of the most troubling misuses of modern software. The primary challenge, he indicated, is addressing harmful cases while preserving the societal benefits created by AI.

Article Title: Elon Musk to NASA's safety watchdog, Aerospace Safety Advisory Panel: Your number is wrong, that's way too ...
Article Text:
What is worrying NASA's security advisory panel

NASA’s safety advisory board Aerospace Safety Advisory Panel has reportedly offered a mixed appraisal of the agency’s deep-space ambitions and low Earth orbit (LEO) logistics, drawing swift public pushback from Spacex CEO Elon Musk over the mechanics of reaching the Moon. During its latest assessment, the Aerospace Safety Advisory Panel (ASAP) cited projections that SpaceX’s Starship Human Landing System (HLS) might require around 22 precursor launches to support a single crewed lunar landing. The staggering launch tempo is driven by orbital refueling requirements, a stark contrast to the 1960s Apollo program, where a single Saturn V lifted an entire mission payload to the Moon using hypergolic-fueled landers.ASAP member Charlie Precourt, a former NASA astronaut, said that they had been told that 22 launches would be needed to provide the requisite amount of propellant for the lander to reach lunar orbit. Precourt also noted NASA is requiring only one uncrewed test to demonstrate the HLS can land, followed by an engine restart. Musk rejected the panel’s launch estimate on social media platform X. "That's way too high," Musk stated, countering that the "actual number will be more like 6 to 8. "As reported by The Register, transferring super-chilled cryogenic propellant between vehicles at an unprecedented scale remains an unproven pillar of the Artemis architecture.To date, SpaceX has executed one Starship flight to orbit. If the panel's higher estimate proves closer to reality, the operational cadence required to stage a Moon mission will present a steep engineering and logistical hurdle.The scrutiny arrives as NASA balances high political stakes with shifting timelines. While Artemis III has been rescoped into a 2027 low Earth orbit demonstration of competing lunar lander technologies from SpaceX and Blue Origin, pressure persists to land astronauts on the lunar surface before the end of the Trump administration.“We’re going to recommend that NASA re-examine the mission objectives, potentially the system architecture for Artemis IV and the subsequent missions, to establish a more balanced approach to risk, prioritize the objectives-driven planning, and maintain a consistent cadence of flight missions," said Charlie Precourt. Further added, “For every test objective, including objectives related to uncrewed demonstration missions by the lander system coming from the service providers, NASA should develop a detailed plan for testing and data collection, incorporating both ground and flight tests to ensure that all risks are thoroughly identified and mitigated. This structured approach will provide a more balanced sequence of flight tests, ultimately supporting a successful crewed lunar landing and the creation of a sustainable lunar base.”Beyond the Moon, the panel also raised alarms about NASA’s reliance on the commercial sector for access to low Earth orbit (LEO). While ASAP lauded progress toward the crewed Artemis II lunar flyby and praised NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman, it reportedly highlighted a looming vulnerability: Spacex's intention to eventually retire its workhorse Falcon 9 rockets and Crew Dragon spacecraft. A phase-out could complicate efforts to extend operations aboard the International Space Station (ISS) and cloud the deployment of the planned ISS deorbit vehicle. ASAP said that they will soon open a new recommendation to Isaacman about how to proceed with Artemis to ensure safety.The prospect of losing Dragon is said to be exacerbated by ongoing delays surrounding Boeing’s Starliner. While a potential uncrewed test flight had been floated for late 2026, the safety panel noted the mission has slipped to mid-January 2027 at the earliest, with the schedule remaining under active review.Should Dragon retire before another viable domestic system matures, NASA could be left solely dependent on Starliner for commercial crew rotation -- upending the agency's long-sought goal of redundant US providers.The pressure on cargo resupply is similarly tight. If Dragon's cargo variant departs, Northrop Grumman’s Cygnus spacecraft stands as the sole domestic alternative, supplemented internationally by Japan’s upcoming HTV-X. While Russia continues routine rotations using Soyuz crew capsules and Progress freighters, NASA reportedly remains committed to preserving independent, continuous American access to orbit.
Article Summary: NASA's safety advisory board Aerospace Safety Advisory Panel has reportedly offered a mixed appraisal of the agency's deep-space ambitions and low Earth orbit (LEO) logistics. The panel cited projections that SpaceX’s Starship Human Landing System (HLS) might require around 22 precursor launches to support a single crewed lunar landing.
